Preface
Welcome to Principles of Macroeconomics: An Institutional and Social Science Perspective.
This textbook offers an analytical, empirical approach to macroeconomic systems, national accounting, business cycles, monetary mechanisms, and fiscal policy. It is structured around the analytical depth of Paul Krugman and Robin Wells (Macroeconomics, 6th ed.) and UC Berkeley Econ 2.

title: 1  Chapter 1: First Principles of Economics & Macroeconomic Systems
text:
Conceptual Introduction
While microeconomics zooms in on how individual households, workers, and firms make decisions in specific markets, macroeconomics steps back to examine the behavior of the entire economy as an interconnected system. Macroeconomists study economy-wide phenomena: why total national output (Real GDP) grows over decades, why recessions occasionally trigger widespread unemployment, what causes sustained inflation, and how central banks and governments use monetary and fiscal policies to stabilize economic fluctuations.
A foundational insight of macroeconomics is that the whole is more than the simple sum of its parts. In an economy where people and businesses buy from and sell to one another, one person’s spending is another person’s income. When many households or businesses change their behavior at the same time, feedback can produce aggregate outcomes different from what any individual intended—a possibility economists call the fallacy of composition.
The Paradox of Thrift is one possible short-run feedback mechanism. For an individual household facing financial uncertainty, cutting consumption and saving more may be prudent. If many households do this together, however, business sales can fall, reducing production, hiring, and household income. In a model with spare capacity, slow price adjustment, and no offsetting increase in investment or public spending, aggregate income may fall enough that total saving does not rise as intended. This result depends on those assumptions; it is not a universal prediction for every economy or time horizon.


Visual Representation
Figure 1 summarizes this conditional short-run feedback loop: lower consumption can reduce business revenue and household income, reinforcing efforts to save.






NoteClear It Up: Fallacy of Composition in Macroeconomics



What is true for a single individual is not automatically true for the whole economy at once. If one fan stands up at a stadium concert, they get a better view; if everyone stands up simultaneously, nobody sees better and everyone’s legs get tired. Similarly, if every firm cuts wages simultaneously to boost profits, worker purchasing power falls and consumer demand for those firms’ products shrinks.





Figure 1. A possible short-run feedback in the Paradox of Thrift. The mechanism assumes spare capacity and no immediate offset from investment or policy; actual outcomes depend on economic conditions.




Real-World Application: The 2008–2009 Great Recession and Household Deleveraging
The Great Recession offers a case for distinguishing a model mechanism from a historical explanation. When households try to repair balance sheets by cutting consumption, the short-run model predicts weaker sales and income if other spending does not offset the decline. Jones, Midrigan, and Philippon (2022) evaluate the household-leverage explanation and find that credit shocks account for only a small fraction of the aggregate employment decline in 2008–2010, while slowing the recovery. The saving-spending mechanism is useful for organizing the question, but it does not by itself establish the cause or size of a historical downturn.


Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
For the worked model, assume a closed economy with no government or foreign trade, fixed prices, spare productive capacity, fixed planned investment, and a constant marginal propensity to consume. If consumption depends on autonomous spending \(C_0\) and a fraction \(c\) of income \(Y\), private saving is \(S=Y-C\):
\[
C = C_0 + cY, \qquad S = Y - (C_0 + cY) = -C_0 + (1 - c)Y
\]
In this model’s equilibrium, planned saving equals planned investment (\(S=I_p\)). The setup illustrates a short-run possibility rather than a universal response.
Worked Problem: Suppose a closed economy has planned business investment fixed at \(I_p = \$200\text{ billion}\), and households initially consume according to \(C = 100 + 0.75Y\) (so initial saving is \(S = -100 + 0.25Y\)).

Find initial equilibrium national income \(Y_1^*\) and confirm that equilibrium saving equals \(\$200\text{ billion}\).
Suppose consumer anxiety causes households to cut autonomous consumption by \(\$50\text{ billion}\) (trying to save \(\$50\text{ billion}\) more at every income level), so \(C_{\text{new}} = 50 + 0.75Y\) and \(S_{\text{new}} = -50 + 0.25Y\). Compute the new equilibrium income \(Y_2^*\) and new total saving \(S_2^*\).

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Solve for Initial Equilibrium Income (\(Y_1^*\)) Where \(S = I_p\):

\[
-100 + 0.25Y_1^* = 200 \implies 0.25Y_1^* = 300 \implies Y_1^* = \mathbf{\$1{,}200\text{ billion}}
\]
Check equilibrium saving: \(S_1^* = -100 + 0.25(1{,}200) = -100 + 300 = \mathbf{\$200\text{ billion}}\).

Solve for New Equilibrium Income (\(Y_2^*\)) After the Saving Surge: Set \(S_{\text{new}} = I_p\):

\[
-50 + 0.25Y_2^* = 200 \implies 0.25Y_2^* = 250 \implies Y_2^* = \mathbf{\$1{,}000\text{ billion}}
\]
Check new equilibrium saving at \(Y_2^* = \$1{,}000\):
\[
S_2^* = -50 + 0.25(1{,}000) = -50 + 250 = \mathbf{\$200\text{ billion}}
\]
Conclusion: Under the stated assumptions, the \(\$50\) billion reduction in autonomous consumption lowers equilibrium income by \(\$200\) billion (from \(\$1{,}200\) billion to \(\$1{,}000\) billion), while equilibrium saving remains \(\$200\) billion. This is the paradox-of-thrift result for this model.

title: 1  Chapter 1: First Principles of Economics & Macroeconomic Systems
section: 1.2 The Expanded Circular Flow, Leakages, and Injections
text:
1.2 The Expanded Circular Flow, Leakages, and Injections

Conceptual Introduction
To track how dollars circulate across an open economy, macroeconomists add three sectors to the household-firm circular flow: the financial sector, which connects savers and borrowers; government, which collects taxes and purchases goods and services; and the rest of the world, which buys exports and sells imports.
In this four-sector accounting framework, expenditure on domestically produced final goods and services (\(Y\)) equals four spending components:
\[
Y \equiv C + I + G + NX, \qquad \text{where } NX = X - M
\]
Here \(C\) is household consumption, \(I\) is private investment spending, \(G\) is government purchases of goods and services, and \(NX\) is net exports (exports \(X\) minus imports \(M\)).
Three flows are called leakages: private saving (\(S\)), net taxes (\(T\)), and imports (\(M\)). Three flows are called injections: investment (\(I\)), government purchases (\(G\)), and exports (\(X\)). In the accounting equilibrium represented here, total leakages equal total injections:
\[
S + T + M = I + G + X
\]


Visual Representation
Figure 2 maps the expanded four-sector circular flow, distinguishing leakage channels (\(S, T, M\)) from injection channels (\(I, G, X\)) by both label and line style.



Figure 2. The Four-Sector Macroeconomic Circular Flow. Dashed orange arrows show leakages (\(S+T+M\)); solid teal arrows show injections (\(I+G+X\)).




Real-World Application: U.S. Budget Deficits and Trade Balances
Rearranging the leakage-injection identity \(S + T + M = I + G + X\) yields the fundamental open-economy accounting relation:
\[
(S - I) + (T - G) = (X - M) = NX
\]
Here \((S-I)\) is the private sector’s net saving balance and \((T-G)\) is public saving (a government budget surplus if positive, or deficit if negative). If public saving and private net saving are both negative, the identity implies \(NX<0\). This is an accounting relationship, not proof that a budget deficit causes a trade deficit; the private, public, and foreign balances are jointly linked.


Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
Balancing total leakages against total injections confirms the expenditure identity:
\[
S + T + M = I + G + X \iff Y = C + I + G + (X - M)
\]
Worked Problem: In a macroeconomic model of an open economy (in billions of dollars), household consumption is \(C = \$900\), private saving is \(S = \$250\), net taxes are \(T = \$350\), government purchases are \(G = \$400\), private investment is \(I = \$300\), exports are \(X = \$200\), and imports are \(M = \$300\).

Verify that total leakages equal total injections.
Compute national income (\(Y\)) using both the income-disposition identity (\(Y = C + S + T\)) and the aggregate expenditure identity (\(Y = C + I + G + NX\)).

Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Compare Total Leakages and Total Injections:

\[
\text{Total Leakages} = S + T + M = \$250 + \$350 + \$300 = \mathbf{\$900\text{ billion}}
\]
\[
\text{Total Injections} = I + G + X = \$300 + \$400 + \$200 = \mathbf{\$900\text{ billion}}
\]
Total leakages equal total injections (\(\$900\text{B} = \$900\text{B}\)).

Compute National Income (\(Y\)) via Both Identities:

\[
Y_{\text{income}} = C + S + T = \$900 + \$250 + \$350 = \mathbf{\$1{,}500\text{ billion}}
\]
\[
NX = X - M = \$200 - \$300 = -\$100\text{ billion}
\]
\[
Y_{\text{expenditure}} = C + I + G + NX = \$900 + \$300 + \$400 + (-\$100) = \mathbf{\$1{,}500\text{ billion}}
\]
Conclusion: Both accounting views yield the exact same national income of \(\$1{,}500\text{ billion}\).

title: 1  Chapter 1: First Principles of Economics & Macroeconomic Systems
section: 1.3 Business Cycles, Stabilization Policy, and Long-Run Growth
text:
1.3 Business Cycles, Stabilization Policy, and Long-Run Growth

Conceptual Introduction
If you trace U.S. Real GDP over the past century, two distinct patterns jump off the page: a steady upward trend across decades, interrupted periodically by jagged waves of expansion and contraction. Macroeconomists divide their discipline around these two horizons:

The Business Cycle (Short-Run Fluctuations): Alternating periods of economic expansion (rising output and falling unemployment) and recession (a broad downturn in output, income, and employment). The turning point from expansion to recession is a peak, and the bottom turning point where recovery begins is a trough.
Long-Run Economic Growth: The sustained upward trend in an economy’s potential productive capacity over decades, which determines long-run living standards across generations.

To smooth out painful short-run business cycles without derailing long-run growth, policymakers deploy two stabilization toolkits: fiscal policy (changes in federal government spending and tax rates enacted by Congress and the President) and monetary policy (changes in interest rates and financial conditions implemented by the Federal Reserve).


Visual Representation
Figure 3 is a schematic—not a data series—showing output fluctuating around a rising long-run trend, with illustrative peaks, troughs, contractions, and recoveries.



Figure 3. Schematic Business Cycle. The solid orange line represents illustrative output fluctuations around a dashed long-run trend; it is not observed U.S. GDP data.




Real-World Application: NBER Business Cycle Dating
In the United States, the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) Business Cycle Dating Committee identifies peaks and troughs using a broad set of indicators. It emphasizes economy-wide measures and notes there is no fixed rule about which indicators receive weight; a recession is not determined solely by a two-quarter GDP rule (NBER, n.d.).


Mathematical Foundation (Algebra Level)
The percentage output gap measures how far actual Real GDP (\(Y\)) deviates from estimated Potential GDP (\(Y^*\)):
\[
\text{Output Gap } (\%) = \frac{Y - Y^*}{Y^*} \times 100\%
\]
Worked Problem: For an illustrative calculation, suppose estimated Potential Real GDP is \(Y^*=\$25.0\) trillion and actual Real GDP is \(Y=\$24.2\) trillion. Compute the dollar output gap and the percentage output gap. Potential GDP is estimated rather than directly observed.
Step-by-Step Breakdown:

Compute the Dollar Output Gap (\(Y - Y^*\)):

\[
Y - Y^* = \$24.2\text{ trillion} - \$25.0\text{ trillion} = \mathbf{-\$0.8\text{ trillion}\ (-\$800\text{ billion})}
\]

Compute the Percentage Output Gap:

\[
\text{Output Gap } (\%) = \frac{-0.8}{25.0} \times 100\% = -0.032 \times 100\% = \mathbf{-3.2\%}
\]
Conclusion: In this example, actual output is \(3.2\%\) below estimated potential output, a dollar gap of \(\$800\) billion.






NoteOptional Advanced Section: Hodrick-Prescott Trend Decomposition



Note for Economics Majors and Quantitative Students: The Hodrick–Prescott filter decomposes observed log Real GDP \(y_t=\ln(Y_t)\) into a smooth trend \(\tau_t\) and a residual component \(c_t=y_t-\tau_t\) by solving:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\min_{\{\tau_t\}} \quad
&\sum_{t=1}^{T} (y_t - \tau_t)^2 \\
&+ \lambda \sum_{t=2}^{T-1}
\left[ (\tau_{t+1} - \tau_t) - (\tau_t - \tau_{t-1}) \right]^2
\end{aligned}
\]
For quarterly data, \(\lambda=1{,}600\) is a widely used convention (Hodrick and Prescott, 1997). The residual is not automatically stationary, and the filtered trend is not a direct observation of potential GDP.




Selected References

National Bureau of Economic Research. “Business Cycle Dating.” https://www.nber.org/research/business-cycle-dating
Jones, Callum, Virgiliu Midrigan, and Thomas Philippon. 2022. “Household Leverage and the Recession.” Econometrica 90(5): 2471–2505. NBER Working Paper 16965. https://www.nber.org/papers/w16965
Hodrick, Robert J., and Edward C. Prescott. 1997. “Postwar U.S. Business Cycles: An Empirical Investigation.” Journal of Money, Credit and Banking 29(1): 1–16. https://doi.org/10.2307/2953682

These objectives support MA-1 and C2002-1. Key terms include relative price, price index, inflation, nominal value, real value, and purchasing power.

title: 3  Chapter 3: Supply and Demand: Macroeconomic Foundations
section: 3.2 One Price Changes, or the Price Level Changes?
text:
3.2 One Price Changes, or the Price Level Changes?
Suppose the price of a hospital visit rises while prices of most other goods are stable. That is a change in a relative price: medical care has become more expensive compared with the rest of the consumption basket. A family may respond by using insurance, choosing another provider, or postponing care. The change guides choices and reallocates resources in that market, but by itself it is not economy-wide inflation.
Inflation is a sustained increase in a broad price index. It reduces the purchasing power of a nominal dollar if the dollar amount does not rise with prices. A one-time increase in a single price may contribute to an index, but it does not establish that the general price level is accelerating. Similarly, a temporary price-level increase is not the same thing as an ongoing inflation rate.
crumbs: 3  Chapter 3: Supply and Demand: Macroeconomic Foundations

title: 3  Chapter 3: Supply and Demand: Macroeconomic Foundations
section: 3.3 Graph Description: Relative Price and a Broad Index
text:
3.3 Graph Description: Relative Price and a Broad Index
To compare price movements over time, put time on the horizontal axis and index values on the vertical axis. Set both series to 100 in a chosen base month. One line tracks the price index for a particular category, such as medical care; the other tracks the all-items CPI. If the medical-care line rises faster, its relative price has increased over that interval. If both rise at the same rate, the relative price is roughly unchanged even though nominal prices have risen. Indexing the series makes proportional changes comparable; it does not put different baskets on the same dollar scale.
The economic distinction is between a movement in one component’s price and a change in the overall index. A demand or supply shift in one product market changes that market’s equilibrium price; economy-wide inflation requires broad price changes and a sustained process, not a relabeling of one relative-price shock.
crumbs: 3  Chapter 3: Supply and Demand: Macroeconomic Foundations

title: 3  Chapter 3: Supply and Demand: Macroeconomic Foundations
section: 3.4 Price Indexes, Inflation, and Real Values
text:
3.4 Price Indexes, Inflation, and Real Values
A price index compares the cost of a defined basket in one period with its cost in a reference period. The percentage inflation rate between periods \(t-1\) and \(t\) is:
\[
\pi_t=\frac{P_t-P_{t-1}}{P_{t-1}}\times 100\%.
\]
To express a nominal amount in the purchasing power of a selected base period, rescale it by the ratio of the base-period index to the current index:
\[
X^{\text{real, base}}_t=X^{\text{nominal}}_t\frac{P_{\text{base}}}{P_t}.
\]
When the index base is 100, this is commonly written as nominal value times \(100/P_t\). Real values answer a purchasing-power question; nominal values answer how many current dollars changed hands. Neither measure is universally preferable: use the one suited to the question.






TipFRED Data: Medical Care and the CPI



FRED series CPIAUCSL is the all-items Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers: U.S. City Average, monthly and seasonally adjusted, with 1982-1984=100. CPIMEDSL is the corresponding medical-care index with the same base and frequency. Comparing their percentage changes can illustrate how a component’s price movement differs from the overall basket. The CPI reflects a weighted urban-consumer basket, not every household’s exact spending pattern; the comparison is descriptive and does not by itself identify why prices changed.








NoteClear It Up: A Price Increase Is Not Automatically Inflation



A rise in one product’s price changes that product’s relative price. Inflation refers to a sustained rise in a broad price index. Also keep nominal and real values distinct: a nominal wage can rise while its real purchasing power falls if the price level rises faster.

title: 3  Chapter 3: Supply and Demand: Macroeconomic Foundations
text:
3.5 Check Your Understanding

If a nominal wage rises by 3 percent while the relevant price index rises by 5 percent, what happens approximately to its purchasing power?
Why is a rise in the price of one service not sufficient evidence of economy-wide inflation?
What does rebasing two indexes to 100 help compare, and what does it not make identical?

Answers: (1) Real purchasing power falls by roughly 2 percent, using the small-change approximation. (2) It may be a relative-price change confined to that market. (3) It compares proportional changes; it does not make the baskets or dollar costs identical.

4.1 Learning Outcomes and Key Terms

These objectives support MA-1 and C2002-1. Key terms include final good, intermediate good, value added, consumption, investment, government purchases, net exports, nominal GDP, real GDP, and GDP deflator.

title: 4  Chapter 4: Macroeconomic Variables: Measuring Output and GDP
section: 4.2 What GDP Counts: A Chip in a Computer
text:
4.2 What GDP Counts: A Chip in a Computer
Imagine a processor sold to a computer maker and then installed in a new laptop. Counting the processor’s full sale and the laptop’s full sale would count some production twice. National accounts avoid this by counting final output or summing each firm’s value added. The processor maker contributes the value of its output minus intermediate inputs; the computer maker contributes the laptop’s value minus purchased components. GDP measures the market value of final goods and services produced within a country’s borders during a period, not the value of every financial transaction or every useful activity.
GDP excludes purchases of existing assets, such as a used home, because that production occurred earlier. It also excludes transfers such as Social Security benefits from government purchases: transfers redistribute income but are not direct purchases of current output. Newly produced residential construction is counted as investment, while a household’s purchase of the same house from another household is an asset transfer.
crumbs: 4  Chapter 4: Macroeconomic Variables: Measuring Output and GDP

title: 4  Chapter 4: Macroeconomic Variables: Measuring Output and GDP
text:
4.3 Three Equivalent Accounting Views
The expenditure approach adds spending on final domestic production:
\[
Y=C+I+G+NX, \qquad NX=X-M.
\]
\(C\) is household consumption, \(I\) is gross private domestic investment (including inventory change and new residential construction), \(G\) is government purchases of goods and services, and \(NX\) is exports minus imports. Imports are subtracted because they may already be included in \(C\), \(I\), or \(G\) but were produced abroad.
The production or value-added approach sums each producer’s value added, avoiding double counting. The income approach sums incomes generated in domestic production, including compensation of employees, proprietors’ income, rental income, corporate profits, net interest, taxes on production and imports less subsidies, and consumption of fixed capital. GDP and gross domestic income (GDI) should be equal in principle because one producer’s output is another party’s expenditure and income; measured estimates can differ because of data sources and timing. The statistical discrepancy records that difference rather than implying two different economies.
crumbs: 4  Chapter 4: Macroeconomic Variables: Measuring Output and GDP

title: 4  Chapter 4: Macroeconomic Variables: Measuring Output and GDP
section: 4.4 Nominal GDP, Real GDP, and the Deflator
text:
4.4 Nominal GDP, Real GDP, and the Deflator
Nominal GDP values current production at current-period prices. If both quantities and prices rise, nominal GDP can rise even when physical output does not. Real GDP values production using a chain-type quantity index designed to remove price changes. The GDP implicit price deflator is:
\[
ext{GDP Deflator}_t=\frac{\text{Nominal GDP}_t}{\text{Real GDP}_t}\times 100.
\]
Its percent change approximates price change for domestically produced final output. It is not the same basket as the CPI, which focuses on prices paid by urban consumers and includes imports in the consumer basket.






TipFRED Data: Current-Dollar and Chained-Dollar GDP



FRED’s GDP series reports Gross Domestic Product in billions of current dollars at a seasonally adjusted annual rate, quarterly. GDPC1 reports real GDP in billions of chained 2017 dollars at a seasonally adjusted annual rate, quarterly. The series titles and units matter: compare changes over time using the appropriate real measure, and do not read chained-dollar levels as current-dollar spending. Both series are revised as the BEA incorporates new source data.








NoteClear It Up: Investment Is Not a Stock Purchase



In GDP accounting, investment means newly produced capital goods, new residential structures, and inventory accumulation. Buying an existing share of stock is a financial transaction, not current production, so it is not counted as \(I\) in GDP.
crumbs: 4  Chapter 4: Macroeconomic Variables: Measuring Output and GDP

title: 4  Chapter 4: Macroeconomic Variables: Measuring Output and GDP
text:
4.5 Check Your Understanding

Why are imported goods subtracted in \(NX\) even though consumers and firms buy them?
If nominal GDP rises while real GDP is unchanged, what has happened to the GDP deflator?
Why does counting a final laptop and every component’s full sale overstate output?

Answers: (1) Imports were produced abroad and must be removed from domestic production. (2) The deflator rises. (3) It double-counts intermediate production; use final value or value added.

title: 5  Chapter 5: Employment, Unemployment Metrics, and the Price Level
text:
5.1 Learning Outcomes and Key Terms
By the end of this chapter, students should be able to classify people in the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) household-survey framework; calculate labor-force participation, employment-population, U-3, and U-6 rates; interpret unemployment and vacancy movements over the business cycle; estimate an illustrative output loss with Okun’s law; and distinguish nominal wage growth from changes in real purchasing power. These goals support MA-1 and C2002-1. Key terms include civilian noninstitutional population, labor force, not in the labor force, marginally attached, underemployment, U-3, U-6, Beveridge curve, potential output, CPI, and real wage.
crumbs: 5  Chapter 5: Employment, Unemployment Metrics, and the Price Level

title: 5  Chapter 5: Employment, Unemployment Metrics, and the Price Level
text:
5.2 Part 1: The BLS Population Map

5.2.1 Bring It Home: One Person, One Survey Week
Imagine that a worker’s restaurant closes for renovations during the BLS survey reference week. The worker did no paid work that week, is available to return, and has not searched elsewhere because the employer expects the temporary layoff to end. Another person worked a paid shift for a delivery platform, even though the work was only a few hours. A third person wants a job but stopped searching after repeated rejections. These people may all describe themselves as needing more work, but the household survey classifies them differently using consistent rules.
The starting population is the civilian noninstitutional population (CNIP) age 16 and older, denoted \(P\). The BLS partitions it into people in the labor force and people not in the labor force:
\[
P = LF + NILF, \qquad LF = E + U.
\]
Here \(E\) is employed, \(U\) is unemployed, \(LF\) is the labor force, and \(NILF\) is not in the labor force. A person is employed if they did any work for pay or profit during the reference week, worked without pay in a family business under the survey threshold, or had a job but were temporarily absent. A person is unemployed if they had no job, were available for work, and actively searched in the prior four weeks; people on temporary layoff are treated under a specific exception. Everyone else in \(P\) is classified as not in the labor force.


5.2.2 Graph Description: The BLS Classification Tree
Picture a flowchart rather than a graph with a behavioral curve. At the top is the full rectangle \(P\). A vertical split separates \(LF\) on the left from \(NILF\) on the right. The \(LF\) rectangle splits again into \(E\) and \(U\). Every person belongs to exactly one leaf of this tree for the survey classification. The categories describe survey status, not a person’s worth, effort, or need for income.


5.2.3 Work It Out: Rates Have Different Denominators
Suppose a hypothetical local population has \(P=1{,}000\), with \(E=600\), \(U=40\), and therefore \(NILF=360\). First add employed and unemployed people to find the labor force: \[\begin{align}
LF &= E+U = 600+40=640,\\
u_3 &= \frac{U}{LF}\times 100\% = \frac{40}{640}\times100\%=6.25\%,\\
LFPR &= \frac{LF}{P}\times100\% = \frac{640}{1{,}000}\times100\%=64\%,\\
EPOP &= \frac{E}{P}\times100\% = \frac{600}{1{,}000}\times100\%=60\%.
\end{align}\] The unemployment rate is not the share of the entire population without a job. Its denominator is the labor force. The participation rate asks what share of the population is working or actively seeking work; the employment-population ratio asks what share is employed.






NoteClear It Up: A Falling U-3 Rate Can Hide a Falling Labor Force



If unemployed people stop searching, they generally move from \(U\) to \(NILF\). That lowers both the numerator and denominator of U-3 and can make the rate fall without any new hiring. Check \(LFPR\) and \(EPOP\) alongside unemployment before concluding that job conditions improved.
crumbs: 5  Chapter 5: Employment, Unemployment Metrics, and the Price Level

title: 5  Chapter 5: Employment, Unemployment Metrics, and the Price Level
section: 5.3 Part 2: U-3, U-6, and the Gig Economy
text:
5.3 Part 2: U-3, U-6, and the Gig Economy

5.3.1 The Headline Rate and Broader Underutilization
U-3 is the official unemployment rate: unemployed people as a share of the civilian labor force. It is useful, comparable, and deliberately narrow. It does not count people who want a job but have not searched recently, and it counts a person working part time as employed even if that person wants full-time hours.
U-6 is a broader BLS measure of labor underutilization. It includes the unemployed, people marginally attached to the labor force, and people employed part time for economic reasons. Marginally attached people want and are available for work, searched sometime in the prior 12 months, but did not search during the most recent four weeks. Discouraged workers are one subset of the marginally attached. U-6’s denominator adds the marginally attached to the labor force, so the numerator and denominator must be expanded together:
\[
U\text{-}6 =
\frac{U + M + PT_{econ}}{LF + M}\times100\%,
\]
where \(M\) is marginally attached people and \(PT_{econ}\) is employed part-time for economic reasons.


5.3.2 Bring It Home: A Platform Worker Wants More Hours
A courier completes several paid deliveries during the reference week and wants a stable, full-time schedule. Under the household-survey concept, the courier is employed because they performed paid work; being a gig worker does not by itself make someone unemployed. If the courier is working part time for economic reasons and wants full-time hours, they may be included in the U-6 numerator but not in U-3’s unemployed count. Another courier who did no work, wants a job, is available, and searched within the last four weeks may be unemployed. A worker who stopped searching may be marginally attached, rather than unemployed under U-3.
The distinction is about measured labor utilization, not whether a gig job is good or bad. The survey classification alone does not reveal earnings volatility, benefits, schedule control, job security, or whether the worker prefers independent contracting. Those are important dimensions of job quality, but they require additional data.


5.3.3 Work It Out: Compare U-3 and U-6
Continue the hypothetical example with \(LF=640\) and \(U=40\). Suppose \(M=20\) people are marginally attached and \(PT_{econ}=30\) employed people want full-time work but can only find part-time hours. Then: \[\begin{align}
U\text{-}3 &= \frac{40}{640}\times100\%=6.25\%,\\
U\text{-}6 &= \frac{40+20+30}{640+20}\times100\%
=\frac{90}{660}\times100\%\approx13.64\%.
\end{align}\] These are illustrative counts, not a current estimate for any city or month. The gap between the measures shows that the headline rate omits forms of underutilization; it does not mean U-3 is incorrectly calculated.






TipFRED Data: Compare Measures, Not Just Headlines



FRED distributes official BLS series including UNRATE (U-3), U6RATE (U-6), CIVPART (labor-force participation rate), and EMRATIO (employment-population ratio). These are seasonally adjusted monthly percentage series. Plotting them together can show whether a change in U-3 coincides with movement in broader underutilization or participation. The rates have different definitions and denominators; their difference is informative, not an arithmetic error.

section: 5.4 Part 3: Vacancies, Unemployment, and Output Slack
text:
5.4 Part 3: Vacancies, Unemployment, and Output Slack

5.4.1 The Beveridge Curve
The Beveridge curve describes the usual inverse relationship between the unemployment rate and the job-vacancy rate. In a Cartesian diagram, place unemployment \(u\) (percent) on the horizontal axis and vacancies \(v\) (percent) on the vertical axis. A movement down and left is consistent with a stronger matching environment: vacancies rise as unemployment falls. A movement up and right is consistent with weaker labor demand: vacancies fall as unemployment rises. This is a descriptive relationship, not a mechanical law.
The curve can shift. Improved matching, geographic mobility, or training can move the relationship inward, allowing more hires for a given vacancy rate. Mismatch between workers’ skills and open jobs, search frictions, or slower matching can shift it outward. A point on the curve is an observed combination; a shift is a change in the relationship itself.



Figure 1. A downward-sloping Beveridge relationship and an outward shift associated with weaker matching. Curves and endpoints are shown within the labeled 0–10 percent plotting range.




5.4.2 Okun’s Law: From an Unemployment Gap to an Output Gap
Okun’s law summarizes a regularity: when unemployment is above its sustainable or natural benchmark, real output tends to be below potential. A simplified gap form is:
\[
\frac{Y-Y^*}{Y^*}\approx -\beta(u-u^*), \qquad \beta>0,
\]
where \(Y\) is real output, \(Y^*\) is potential output, \(u\) and \(u^*\) are measured in percentage points, and \(\beta\) is an estimated coefficient. The relationship varies by period and specification. It does not prove that unemployment alone caused a particular output loss.


5.4.3 Work It Out: An Illustrative $1.0 Trillion Output Shortfall
Assume potential real GDP is \(Y^*=\$25.0\) trillion in a chosen base-year dollar measure, actual unemployment is \(u=6\%\), the estimated benchmark is \(u^*=4\%\), and an illustrative Okun coefficient is \(\beta=2\). First find the unemployment gap: \(u-u^*=2\) percentage points. Then estimate the output gap: \[\begin{align}
\frac{Y-Y^*}{Y^*} &\approx -2(2\%)=-4\%,\\
Y^*-Y &\approx 0.04\times \$25.0\text{ trillion}
=\$1.0\text{ trillion}.
\end{align}\] The estimated shortfall is $1.0 trillion of real output relative to the assumed potential level. This is a model-based illustration, not a reported current loss. Potential GDP and \(\beta\) are estimates, and the result depends on the units and period used.






NoteOptional Advanced: Markov Job-Finding and Separation Flows



In a two-state model, let \(s\) be the period separation probability from employment to unemployment and \(f\) the job-finding probability from unemployment to employment. At steady state, inflows to unemployment equal outflows: \(s(1-u)=fu\). Solving gives:
\[
u^*=\frac{s}{s+f}.
\]
This result assumes a stable two-state population, constant transition probabilities, and no labor-force entry or exit. It makes the stock-flow logic explicit: a higher separation rate raises steady-state unemployment, while a higher job-finding rate lowers it.








NoteOptional Advanced: State-Space Slack and Growth-Rate Okun Relations



Potential output \(Y_t^*\) and the natural unemployment rate \(u_t^*\) are not directly observed. A state-space approach treats them as latent states inferred from noisy observations. Output slack can be represented as \(x_t=\ln Y_t-\ln Y_t^*\), approximately the percentage output gap for small differences; labor slack can be represented as \(u_t-u_t^*\). Their estimated paths depend on the model and can be revised as new observations arrive.
An alternative growth-difference form is \(\Delta u_t\approx-\kappa(g_{Y,t}-g_{Y,t}^*)\), where \(g_{Y,t}\) is real output growth, \(g_{Y,t}^*\) is potential growth, and \(\kappa>0\) is an estimated response coefficient. Growth above potential tends to reduce unemployment; growth below potential tends to raise it. This is an empirical approximation, not an identity.

section: 5.5 Part 4: CPI Inflation and Real-Wage Purchasing Power
text:
5.5 Part 4: CPI Inflation and Real-Wage Purchasing Power

5.5.1 A Price Index and the Cost of a Basket
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) tracks price changes for a representative consumer basket under the BLS methodology. Inflation over a period is the percentage change in the index:
\[
\pi_t=\frac{CPI_t-CPI_{t-1}}{CPI_{t-1}}\times100\%.
\]
The CPI is an index, not a dollar price and not a perfect measure of every household’s cost of living. Households have different spending patterns, and the index summarizes an average basket using a defined method.


5.5.2 Nominal Wages and Real Purchasing Power
A nominal wage is measured in current dollars. A real wage adjusts for the price level and indicates how much of a reference-period basket that wage can buy:
\[
W^{real}_t=\frac{W^{nom}_t}{CPI_t}\times100,
\]
when the CPI is normalized to 100 in the chosen reference period. If a nominal wage rises more slowly than the CPI, its purchasing power falls even though the dollar wage increased.


5.5.3 Work It Out: A Raise That Does Not Keep Pace with Prices
Suppose an hourly wage rises from $20.00 to $20.80, a 4% increase. Over the same period, the CPI rises from 300 to 315, a 5% increase. Express the new wage in the initial period’s purchasing power: \[\begin{align}
W^{real}_0 &= \frac{\$20.00}{300}\times100=\$6.667,\\
W^{real}_1 &= \frac{\$20.80}{315}\times100\approx \$6.603.
\end{align}\] The real wage changes by approximately \((6.603/6.667)-1=-0.95\%\). The worker receives 80 cents more per hour in nominal terms, but the CPI basket costs more, so purchasing power falls slightly.






NoteClear It Up: Nominal Raise Does Not Guarantee a Real Raise



Compare growth rates, not dollar changes alone. When nominal wage growth is below inflation, real wage growth is negative. When the two rates are close, the approximation \(g_{real}\approx g_W-\pi\) is useful, but exact compounding gives a slightly different result.








NoteOptional Advanced: Exact Fisher Compounding for Real Wages



The exact relation between nominal wage growth \(g_W\), inflation \(\pi\), and real wage growth \(g_{real}\) is:
\[
1+g_{real}=\frac{1+g_W}{1+\pi},
\qquad
g_{real}=\frac{1+g_W}{1+\pi}-1.
\]
For \(g_W=0.04\) and \(\pi=0.05\), exact real growth is \(1.04/1.05-1\approx-0.00952\), or about \(-0.95\%\). The subtraction approximation gives \(4\%-5\%=-1\%\). The difference is small here but matters when rates are large.








TipFRED Data: Track Inflation and Real-Wage Context



FRED series CPIAUCSL is the seasonally adjusted U.S. all-items CPI for all urban consumers, reported monthly as an index with 1982–84=100. UNRATE and U6RATE report U-3 and U-6, while CIVPART and EMRATIO provide participation and employment-population context. To study purchasing power, compare nominal wage growth with CPI inflation over matching dates and frequencies; do not divide a wage by an index without stating the chosen base convention.

title: 6  Chapter 6: Saving, Investment Spending, and the Financial System
section: 6.2 Saving Is a Flow; Wealth Is a Stock
text:
6.2 Saving Is a Flow; Wealth Is a Stock

Conceptual Introduction
When you receive a paycheck and decide to put some of it in a savings account, you are saving. Saving is the flow of income not spent over a period (a week, month, or year). By contrast, wealth is the stock of assets you hold at a specific point in time. This distinction matters because confusing flows and stocks is a common source of error in macroeconomic accounting. A household that saves $500 this month adds to its wealth, but the saving itself is a flow: it accumulates wealth over time. Likewise, in macroeconomics, investment refers to spending on newly produced capital goods (buildings, equipment, software) and inventory additions during a period. It does not refer to buying an existing house (which is an asset transfer, not new capital creation) or purchasing a stock certificate (which transfers ownership of an existing firm).


Real-World Application: The U.S. Personal Savings Rate
During the 2008 financial crisis, U.S. household saving jumped from 2% of disposable income to above 6%, as consumers faced falling home values and stock portfolios and rebuilt their wealth buffers. By 2024, after a decade of recovery, the U.S. personal savings rate had settled around 4%—above the pre-crisis average. This variation in the saving flow shows how households respond to wealth shocks (stock market crashes, housing busts) and income uncertainty by altering their current consumption behavior. Understanding whether households are building or depleting wealth (the stock) requires tracking saving flows quarter by quarter.


Mathematical Foundation: Defining Saving and Wealth
If disposable income in a given period is \(Y_d\) and consumption spending is \(C\), then saving \(S\) is:
\[
S = Y_d - C.
\]
Over time, cumulative saving adds to the household’s total wealth \(W\). If a household had wealth \(W_0\) at the start of the year and saves \(S\) during the year, then:
\[
W_{\text{end of year}} = W_0 + S.
\]
Example: If a household starts with $100,000 in savings, earns $60,000 in disposable income, and spends $55,000, then:

Saving during the year: \(S = 60,000 - 55,000 = 5,000\) dollars.
Ending wealth: \(W = 100,000 + 5,000 = 105,000\) dollars.


Figure 1: Saving Flows vs. Wealth Stocks



Figure 1: Annual Saving Flows and Cumulative Wealth Stocks Over Time


This timeline visualization contrasts the flow of annual saving (bars, in CourseOrange) with the accumulating wealth stock (line, in CourseBlue). The chart demonstrates how consistent positive saving flows compound into growing wealth over time, illustrating the fundamental distinction between flows (period-based) and stocks (point-in-time).

title: 6  Chapter 6: Saving, Investment Spending, and the Financial System
section: 6.3 National Saving and the Open-Economy Identity
text:
6.3 National Saving and the Open-Economy Identity

Conceptual Introduction
Just as individuals have saving and wealth, so too do nations. National saving is the total saving of all households, businesses, and government combined. It is a critical variable for understanding how a country finances its investment in new capital and whether it must borrow from abroad. When national saving exceeds domestic investment, a nation is a net lender to the rest of the world—its residents are exporting capital. When investment exceeds saving, the nation must borrow from abroad to finance its investment, creating a current-account deficit. This balance between saving and investment determines whether a country’s foreign debt is growing or shrinking.


The Expenditure Identity and National Saving
Start with the expenditure identity \(Y=C+I+G+NX\). Rearranging gives \(Y-C-G=I+NX\). National saving is \(S=Y-C-G\), so in the simplified model \(S=I+NX\). If net exports are used as the current-account proxy, then \(S-I=NX\): saving above domestic investment corresponds to net lending abroad, while investment above saving is matched by net borrowing from abroad. In full balance-of-payments accounts, the current account includes net primary income and transfers as well as goods and services.
With taxes \(T\) and disposable income \(Y-T\), private saving is \(S_p=Y-T-C\) and public saving is \(S_g=T-G\). National saving adds the two:
\[
S=S_p+S_g=(Y-T-C)+(T-G)=Y-C-G, \qquad S-I=NX \quad\text{(simplified model)}.
\]
In a closed economy, \(NX=0\) and planned national saving equals investment in the accounting identity. The identity does not guarantee that desired saving and planned investment are equal at every interest rate; prices, output, and financial markets adjust toward consistency.


Worked Example: Calculating National Saving and Net Exports
Suppose a closed economy has \(Y = 1{,}000\) billion dollars, \(C = 650\) billion, and \(G = 200\) billion. What is national saving? \[\begin{align*}
S &= Y - C - G \\
&= 1{,}000 - 650 - 200 \\
&= 150 \text{ billion dollars}.
\end{align*}\] In a closed economy, all of this saving must equal domestic investment: \(I = 150\) billion.
Now suppose this is an open economy with the same national income and spending, but investment is higher: \(I = 180\) billion. The identity \(S = I + NX\) implies: \[\begin{align*}
150 &= 180 + NX \\
NX &= 150 - 180 = -30 \text{ billion}.
\end{align*}\] The nation has a trade deficit of $30 billion—it must borrow from abroad to finance the gap between its investment and its saving.

Figure 2: GDP Identity Stacked Bar



Figure 2: Composition of GDP (Y = C + I + G + NX)


This stacked bar chart illustrates how national output is composed of consumption (C), investment (I), government spending (G), and net exports (NX). The visualization clarifies that saving \(S = Y - C - G\) represents the portion of output not consumed or spent by government—the resources available for investment and foreign lending.


Figure 3: Closed vs. Open Economy Accounting



Figure 3: Closed and Open Economy Identities


Side-by-side comparison of: - Closed economy: \(S = I\) (all national saving funds domestic investment) - Open economy: \(S = I + NX\) (saving funds both domestic investment and net foreign investment)



Clear It Up: The Identity Is Not Causation
The accounting relation \(S = I + NX\) must hold by definition. But it does not tell us whether saving caused investment, investment drove income and hence saving, or whether foreign capital inflows led to the current-account deficit. Use a behavioral model (like the loanable-funds market) and empirical evidence to reason about causation.

title: 6  Chapter 6: Saving, Investment Spending, and the Financial System
text:
6.4 Loanable Funds: Graph and Mechanism

Conceptual Introduction
How do saving and investment plans interact to determine the real interest rate? The loanable-funds market is a simple but powerful model for answering this question. In this market, savers supply funds (they lend), and borrowers (firms investing, households buying homes) demand funds (they borrow). The real interest rate—the inflation-adjusted return on lending—is the price that equilibrates the quantity of funds supplied with the quantity demanded. When the real interest rate is too low, the quantity of loanable funds demanded exceeds the quantity supplied, putting upward pressure on the rate. When the rate is too high, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, pushing the rate down. At equilibrium, quantity supplied equals quantity demanded, and the market clears.


Visual Representation: The Loanable-Funds Equilibrium
Put the quantity of loanable funds on the horizontal axis and the real interest rate on the vertical axis. Planned saving is drawn as a supply of funds, often rising with the real return. Planned investment is a demand for funds, often falling as borrowing becomes more expensive. Their intersection is the model’s equilibrium real rate and quantity. A shift in saving or investment plans moves one curve; a change in the interest rate is a movement along a curve. This is a market model, not a literal inventory of all bank deposits.

Figure 4: Loanable Funds Equilibrium



Figure 4: Loanable Funds Market Equilibrium


The supply curve (CourseOrange, upward sloping) represents planned saving as a function of the real interest rate: \(r = 0.5 + 0.025Q\). The demand curve (CourseBlue, downward sloping) represents planned investment: \(r = 6.8 - 0.02Q\). The intersection occurs at equilibrium quantity \(Q^* = 140\) billion dollars and equilibrium rate \(r^* = 4\%\). Dashed guides show the equilibrium coordinates on both axes.



Real-World Application: The 2024 U.S. Loanable-Funds Market
In 2024, the Federal Reserve’s target federal funds rate sat near 5%, keeping the real interest rate (after subtracting expected inflation) in the range of 2%–3%. At these rates, U.S. mortgage rates hovered around 6%–7%, constraining housing demand and new residential investment. Meanwhile, businesses faced higher costs to finance capital projects. This high real interest rate reflects the Fed’s restrictive monetary policy (shifting the demand for loanable funds leftward, as firms reduced borrowing). At the same time, U.S. government deficits were adding to the supply of bonds (shifting the supply of loanable funds, in effect, by crowding out private saving). The interplay of these forces—restrictive monetary policy and fiscal deficits—produced a relatively high equilibrium real interest rate and tighter credit markets.


Mathematical Foundation: Equilibrium in Loanable Funds
Suppose the saving function is \(S = 1 + 0.05 \times Y\) (saving rises with income) and investment demand is \(I = 100 - 10 \times r\) (investment falls as the real interest rate rises). In equilibrium, \(S = I\): \[\begin{align*}
1 + 0.05 \times Y &= 100 - 10 \times r \\
10 \times r &= 99 - 0.05 \times Y \\
r &= 9.9 - 0.005 \times Y.
\end{align*}\] If \(Y = 1{,}000\), then \(r = 9.9 - 5 = 4.9\%\) (approximately 5%). At this rate, the quantity of loanable funds is: \[\begin{align*}
S &= 1 + 0.05 \times 1{,}000 = 51 \text{ (billion)}, \\
I &= 100 - 10 \times 4.9 = 51 \text{ (billion)}.
\end{align*}\] Both saving and investment equal 51 billion—the market clears.


Advanced Optional: Microfoundations of Saving and Investment Decisions
Saving reflects households’ intertemporal choice: they compare consuming today versus consuming tomorrow, weighted by their time preference and the real interest rate. Using Lagrangian optimization:
\[
\mathcal{L} = u(C_1) + \beta u(C_2) + \lambda (Y_1 - C_1 + \frac{Y_2}{1+r} - \frac{C_2}{1+r}),
\]
where \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) are consumption today and tomorrow, \(Y_1\) and \(Y_2\) are income streams, \(\beta\) is the discount factor, and \(r\) is the real interest rate. First-order conditions yield the intertemporal marginal rate of substitution \(MRS = \frac{1+r}{\beta}\), showing that a higher real interest rate encourages current saving (reduces current consumption).
Similarly, firms’ investment decisions reflect the internal rate of return on capital projects. A project with an expected return \(\rho\) is profitable only if \(\rho > r\) (the return exceeds the borrowing cost). As \(r\) rises, fewer projects are profitable, so investment demand falls.

title: 6  Chapter 6: Saving, Investment Spending, and the Financial System
section: 6.5 Deficits, Interest Rates, and Crowding Out
text:
6.5 Deficits, Interest Rates, and Crowding Out

Conceptual Introduction
When a government runs a budget deficit (spending \(G\) exceeds tax revenue \(T\)), it must borrow from the loanable-funds market to finance the gap. This government borrowing increases the demand for loanable funds (or equivalently, reduces the supply available to private borrowers). In a closed economy with a fixed total saving, the government’s borrowing competes with private investment for the available funds. As the government absorbs more of the loanable-funds supply, the real interest rate rises, and some private investment projects that were profitable at the lower rate now become unprofitable. This reduction in private investment due to higher government deficits is called crowding out.
The magnitude of crowding out depends on several factors. If the central bank keeps monetary policy accommodative (low interest rates), deficits need not raise the real interest rate as much. If the economy has slack (unused capacity and unemployment), higher government spending may stimulate income, which can increase saving and partially offset the crowding-out effect. If the economy is open to foreign capital flows, borrowing from abroad can help finance government deficits without crowding out as much domestic investment. Thus, a simple one-for-one crowding-out of investment should not be assumed; real-world responses are more nuanced.


Real-World Application: The U.S. Federal Deficit and Interest Rates (2020–2024)
During the 2020–2021 COVID-19 pandemic, the U.S. government enacted unprecedented fiscal stimulus: the American Rescue Plan (March 2021) authorized $1.9 trillion in spending, bringing total pandemic-related spending to over $5 trillion. This expanded the federal budget deficit sharply. At the same time, the Federal Reserve held its policy rate near zero and engaged in large-scale asset purchases (quantitative easing), keeping market interest rates low. The combination of massive deficit spending and accommodative monetary policy did not produce the textbook crowding-out scenario (rising real rates and collapsing investment) in 2021. Instead, the economy experienced strong nominal growth, elevated inflation, and later, aggressive Fed rate hikes (reaching 5% by 2023). The delay in crowding-out pressures reflected both the Fed’s willingness to supply abundant liquidity and the economy’s sharp rebound from the pandemic shock. By 2024, however, the lingering effects of government deficits and monetary tightening had contributed to higher real interest rates and slower business investment growth.


Worked Example: Quantifying Crowding Out
Suppose initially the saving function is \(S = 50 + 0.1 \times Y\) and investment demand is \(I = 300 - 50 \times r\). With \(Y = 1{,}000\): \[\begin{align*}
S &= 50 + 0.1 \times 1{,}000 = 150 \\
\text{Equilibrium: } 150 &= 300 - 50 \times r \\
50 \times r &= 150 \\
r &= 3\%.
\end{align*}\] Investment at this rate is \(I = 300 - 50 \times 3 = 150\) billion—equilibrium is achieved.
Now suppose a government deficit reduces saving by 50 billion (public saving turns negative). The new saving is \(S' = 50 + 0.1 \times 1{,}000 - 50 = 100\). The new equilibrium is: \[\begin{align*}
100 &= 300 - 50 \times r' \\
50 \times r' &= 200 \\
r' &= 4\%.
\end{align*}\] The real interest rate rises by 1 percentage point. Private investment falls to \(I' = 300 - 50 \times 4 = 100\) billion. The crowding-out effect is a reduction of 50 billion in investment—exactly matching the deficit-driven reduction in saving.

Figure 5: Crowding Out via Supply Shift



Figure 5: Crowding Out in the Loanable Funds Market


Initial equilibrium \(E_1\) occurs at \((Q_1^* = 140 \text{ billion}, r_1^* = 4\%)\). When a government deficit reduces the net supply of loanable funds, the supply curve shifts leftward (CourseOrange to CourseTeal). The new equilibrium \(E_2\) occurs at \((Q_2^* = 130 \text{ billion}, r_2^* = 4.25\%)\). The increase in the real interest rate (\(\Delta r \approx 25\) basis points) chokes off private investment: crowding out of \(\Delta Q \approx 10\) billion. The callout box highlights the crowding-out mechanism: government borrowing competes for available funds, raising borrowing costs for private firms.






NoteKey Insight: The Size of Crowding Out Is Empirical



Textbook models often portray crowding out as one-for-one: each dollar of government deficit reduces private investment by one dollar. In practice, the size of crowding out depends on monetary policy (whether the central bank accommodates the deficit with lower rates), the economy’s slack (unused capacity can absorb stimulus without large rate changes), international capital mobility (foreign investors can help finance the deficit), and the response of private saving to deficits (Ricardian equivalence, a contested hypothesis). The U.S. experience suggests crowding out is real but partial and lagged, unfolding over months or years.




Figure 6: Partial Crowding Out Comparison



Figure 6: Three Scenarios of Crowding Out Magnitude


This figure compares three scenarios illustrating the partial nature of crowding out:

Complete crowding out (left): Supply shifts entirely offset by demand adjustment; ΔI = ΔG
Partial crowding out (center): Interest rate rises moderately; some private investment survives
Monetary accommodation (right): Central bank supplies additional funds; interest rate barely rises

The magnitude of crowding out depends critically on whether the central bank (1) maintains a fixed interest rate by expanding the money supply, (2) allows market rates to adjust freely, or (3) pursues an intermediate path. This explains why deficit spending’s real-economy impacts vary across different monetary-policy regimes.






TipFRED Data: Gross Private Domestic Investment



FRED series GPDI reports gross private domestic investment in billions of current dollars at a seasonally adjusted annual rate, quarterly. It includes fixed investment and inventory change. It is a nominal expenditure flow, not a capital stock and not a direct measure of productive capacity. To study physical investment growth across time, compare an appropriate real series and account for revisions and price changes.








NoteClear It Up: The Identity Is Not a Causal Claim



The accounting relation \(S-I=NX\) in the simplified model must hold ex post. It does not by itself tell us whether saving caused investment, investment caused income and saving, or foreign flows adjusted. Use a behavioral model and evidence to discuss causation.

6.6 Check Your Understanding

If \(Y=1{,}000\), \(C=650\), and \(G=200\), calculate national saving.
If national saving is 150 and investment is 180, what is \(NX\) in the simplified open-economy identity?

In the loanable-funds model, what shifts the supply curve, and what shifts the demand curve?


Answers

\(S=Y-C-G=1{,}000-650-200=150\) billion dollars.
\(NX=S-I=150-180=-30\) billion dollars, a deficit in the simplified model.
No; it transfers ownership of an existing financial asset rather than purchasing newly produced capital. Macroeconomic investment refers only to new capital formation—new buildings, equipment, software, and inventory.
A deficit increases government borrowing, which raises demand for loanable funds (or equivalently, reduces net saving available to the private sector). As the government bids up the price of borrowing (the real interest rate), borrowing becomes more expensive for private firms, reducing private investment—the crowding-out effect.
Supply shifts: changes in household wealth, life-cycle income expectations, taxes, and social safety net generosity shift the saving (supply) curve. Demand shifts: changes in expected business profitability, technology, capital taxes, and uncertainty about returns shift the investment (demand) curve. Changes in the real interest rate cause movements along (not shifts of) the curves.
